lessons.title: Methods Introduction
lessons.summary: As programs grow, writing the same instructions again and again can make the code difficult to read and maintain.

blocks.content: As programs grow, writing the same instructions again and again can make the code difficult to read and maintain.
Suppose a program needs to calculate the delivery charge for several orders. We could write the calculation separately every time:

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.content: If the same calculation is required for many orders, repeating these instructions would make the program unnecessarily long.
Instead, Java allows us to place a group of related instructions inside a method and call that method whenever we need the same task.
Methods help us:

- Reduce repeated code.
- Keep programs organized.
- Make code easier to read and maintain.
Let's learn how to create and use methods next.

lessons.title: Creating a Method
lessons.summary: A method is a named block of code that performs a particular task. Instead of writing the same instructions in different places, we can group them together and reuse them.

blocks.content: A method is a named block of code that performs a particular task. Instead of writing the same instructions in different places, we can group them together and reuse them.
For example, suppose we want to display a short welcome message:

blocks.code:
System.out.println("Welcome to Go Coder!");
System.out.println("Let's start learning Java.");
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.content: These statements belong to the same task, so we can place them inside a method named showWelcome.

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: Here, showWelcome is the method name, while the statements between { and } form the method body.

blocks.content: You may notice void and () in the method declaration. Each part has a specific meaning.
Let's break down the syntax of a method next.

blocks.text: Next, let's see how to call a method so that its code actually runs.

lessons.title: Running a Method
lessons.summary: Writing a method only defines what the program should do. The instructions inside the method run only when the method is called.

lessons.title: Making Methods Flexible
lessons.summary: A method becomes more useful when it can work with different values instead of using the same value every time.

blocks.content: A method becomes more useful when it can work with different values instead of using the same value every time.
For example, a method that always calculates the total of the same two prices is limited. We can make it more flexible by allowing the method to receive input.
In Java methods:

- Argument — a value supplied when calling a method.
- Return value — the result a method sends back to the code that called it.
For example, instead of creating a method that works with only one fixed value, we can design it to accept different values whenever we call it.

lessons.title: The return Statement
lessons.summary: So far, our methods have used void because they only perform an action and don't send a value back.

blocks.content: So far, our methods have used void because they only perform an action and don't send a value back.
But sometimes, we need a method to calculate something and give the result back to the code that called it.
Java provides the return statement for this purpose.
The return statement:

- Sends a value back from the method.
- Immediately stops the method's execution.
- Returns control to the statement where the method was called.
For example, a method can calculate a product and return the result instead of printing it directly.
Let's see how the return statement works in the next example.

lessons.title: Be Careful When Using return
lessons.summary: For example, suppose we create a method that checks a user's account status:

blocks.text: A return statement does not just send a value back—it also ends the method immediately.

blocks.content: For example, suppose we create a method that checks a user's account status:

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.content: The problem is:
Once Java reaches return, the method ends. Therefore, this statement can never run:

blocks.text: Java reports this as an unreachable statement.
Think of return as an exit door:

blocks.code:
Method starts
↓
Execute statements
↓
return value
↓
Method ends immediately
↓
Back to caller
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: So, do not place executable code after a return statement.

blocks.content: This is an important rule to remember when working with methods that return values.

lessons.title: Next Step: Java Methods
lessons.summary: You now know how methods can help you break a program into smaller, reusable tasks.

blocks.content: You now know how methods can help you break a program into smaller, reusable tasks.

- Receive information through arguments.
- Perform a specific operation.
- Send a result back using return.
But methods aren't limited to the ones we create ourselves. Java already provides many ready-to-use methods for common tasks.
In the next section, we'll start working with these standard library methods and see how they can make our programs simpler.

lessons.title: Local Variables
lessons.summary: A variable created inside a method has a limited reach. It belongs only to that method.

A variable declared inside a method is called a local variable.

A local variable belongs to the method where it is declared.
If another method needs its value, return the value instead of trying to access the local variable directly.

blocks.text: This is why understanding local variables and scope is important when working with methods.

lessons.title: Keeping Method Data Separate
lessons.summary: A method can create and use its own temporary variables without exposing them to the rest of the program.

blocks.content: A method can create and use its own temporary variables without exposing them to the rest of the program.
For example, this method calculates the time needed for a trip:

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.content: The hours variable is created only to perform the calculation inside calculateTime().
The main() method doesn't need to know how hours is calculated. It only receives the final value through return.
This separation means we can change the internal calculation without changing the code that calls the method.

blocks.text: Think of a method like a small workspace:

blocks.code:
main()
↓
calculateTime()
├── distance
├── speed
└── hours
↓
return 4
↓
main()
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.content: The variables inside that workspace are local to the method. This keeps different parts of a program from interfering with one another.
